meta.about: Hymns were among the first music Hawaiian choirs sang from printed notes in the 1800s, and hymn singing shaped many later Hawaiian songs. This one is in 3/4: count 1-2-3 and strum the waltz pattern, a thumb note on beat 1 and two light strums. The tune starts on beat 3 with a single pickup note, so the first chord comes on the next downbeat.

meta.title: Andalusian Study
meta.work: A short study on the Andalusian cadence (A minor, G, F, E), written for this course in a Spanish style
meta.arranged: Teddy Rook Book: an original piece; the four-chord descent is a traditional pattern of southern Spanish music
skills: Am, G, F and E chords
an accented strum with a muted chuck
the Spanish sound of G-sharp and F
meta.about: Four chords stepping down, A minor, G, F, E, are the sound of Andalusia in southern Spain, heard in its folk songs and guitar music for centuries. The tune leans on the step from F up to G-sharp, a wide, exotic-sounding step, and always comes to rest on E. Pick the tune first, then strum the chords: a strong accented down strum on beat 1, a muted chuck on beat 3. (Real flamenco strumming, the rasgueado, flicks the fingers out one by one; this strum is a first step toward it.)
meta.source: Original composition by Teddy Rook Book for this course (no source needed); the chord pattern is traditional.

meta.arranged: Teddy Rook Book: clawhammer in double C tuning, moved from D to C and down an octave; a few eighth notes are hammer-ons and the 5th string stands in for one high G
meta.about: A gentle, singing old-time tune, a favorite at jams because the melody is plain and lovely. It sits well in double C tuning (g C G C D): most notes are open strings or the 2nd fret. Every finger stroke falls on a beat; the eighth notes between come from the thumb (on the 5th string, or dropped onto the 3rd string) or from a hammer-on with the left hand. Fiddlers play it in D: put a capo at the 2nd fret (and raise the 5th string to A) to play along with them.

We leave out the pickup notes and start on the downbeat. Every melody note of that version is in our tab at its time (one high G is played on the 5th string, an octave up). Chords are ours. Every half bar is one bum-ditty: strike the melody note on the beat, then brush down on the next beat (the brush always contains that beat’s melody note) and catch the 5th string with your thumb. meta.about: A cheerful old-time song about a simple supper, and one of the first tunes most banjo players learn. Every bar is one bum-ditty: strike the melody note with your fingernail (S), brush down across the top three strings (D), then catch the 5th string with your thumb (T). meta.arranged: Teddy Rook Book: simplified for piano, keeping the bass line and the first violin part of the opening

meta.work: Canon and Gigue in D major for three violins and bass (date unknown, about 1680–1706): the opening
meta.arranged: Teddy Rook Book: the first violin part of the opening for ukulele in low-G tuning, over Pachelbel’s eight chords
skills: moving up the neck to the 5th position
meta.about: Pachelbel’s eight chords, D A Bm F♯m G D G A, repeat every two bars from start to finish: strum them first, one down strum per chord, until they flow. The tune comes in at bar 3, the first violin’s part, slow notes and then eighth notes. Its first notes walk down the 1st string from the 9th fret; in bar 9 the hand moves up to the 9th position for a quick climb to the high A; the low B in bar 8 is the 4th fret of the low G string. Two players sound best here: one strums the chords and the other picks the tune.

meta.title: Prelude in C
meta.work: Méthode complète pour guitare, Op. 59 (1836): Preludes in Progressive Keys, No. 1 in C major
meta.arranged: Teddy Rook Book: Carcassi’s notes as written; the bass is shown as a held half note under the arpeggio, as in the edition. Fingerings and dynamics left out.
skills: C, Am, Dm and G7 shapes
meta.about: Eight bars of broken chords from Carcassi’s guitar method, the kind of short prelude players used to warm up in a new key. Each half bar is one chord: the thumb (p) plays the bass note on the 4th, 5th or 6th string and lets it ring, then the index, middle and ring fingers (i, m, a) play the 3rd, 2nd and 1st strings. Hold the whole chord shape down for the half bar, so every note rings into the next.
meta.source: Mutopia Project edition of Carcassi’s Preludes in Progressive Keys, Op. 59 (entered by Jeffrey Olson from the 1906 Oliver Ditson edition by G. C. Santisteban; public domain). Upper and lower voices read twice and compared with this file note by note.

meta.title: Dry Creek Blues
meta.work: A fingerpicked twelve-bar blues in E, written for this course in the style of the early country blues
meta.arranged: Teddy Rook Book: an original piece with original licks over a steady thumb
meta.about: In the early country blues the thumb is the drummer: it plays a steady beat on the open bass string of the chord (E, A or the B on the 5th string) and never stops, while the fingers play short answering phrases on the top strings. Practice the thumb alone until it runs by itself, then add the fingers one bar at a time. The quick hammer-ons from G to G-sharp, and from G to A in the A bars, give the music its blues sound; the last bar is a turnaround that walks down the 4th string back to B7.
meta.source: Original composition by Teddy Rook Book for this course (no source needed); the twelve-bar form, the steady-thumb style and the turnaround idea are traditional, the licks are our own.

meta.about: One of the oldest American fiddle tunes with a known story: Durang’s violin teacher wrote it for him around 1785, early in his career as a dancer, and it has been played for dancing ever since. The fiddle’s sixteenth notes are our eighth notes; bars 7–8 and the whole B part are an octave lower than the fiddle, and the pickups are left out. meta.arranged: Teddy Rook Book: the tune of the first strain for ukulele, taken from Joplin’s right hand (where he doubles it in octaves, we play the lower note), with chords from his left hand
meta.about: Joplin’s famous rag, published in 1902, more than a decade before the ukulele craze reached the mainland. Ragtime puts tune notes just ahead of the beat and ties them over it: count “1 e and a 2 e and a” and say the tied notes out loud before you play. The jumps in bars 1 and 5, from the open E string up to C at the 3rd fret of the 1st string, are easier than they look. Joplin wrote “Not fast”; we suggest a slower tempo still. To strum, play down-up eighths with a little weight on beat 2.
meta.source: The notes are Joplin’s, from our piano version of The Entertainer, which was checked note by note against the Mutopia Project edition (from a reproduction of the 1902 edition; public domain). We take its first strain once, ending on the chord of the second ending. Our own check compares every tab note with the piano version’s right hand at the same moment.

meta.about: This is the famous opening section, with both of its repeats. The whole piece is a rondo that keeps coming back to this music, and our version ends the way the piece ends. meta.about: Count six eighth notes in each bar, in two groups of three, and feel two slow beats. The tune twice reaches down to B below middle C, which only a low-G ukulele has: the 4th fret of the low G string. Pick the tune with your thumb, keeping your hand still over the first frets. For the chords, strum down-(miss)-up, down-(miss)-up, a lilting 6/8 strum; B7 is the one new shape.

meta.about: One of the great American songs: a gentle, hymn-like tune about remembering people who are going through hard days. It has been sung around campfires and at gatherings for more than 150 years. Learn the tune first (it stays on the top three strings), then strum the chords with the folk strum. When a bar has two or three chords, change on the beat the chord line shows, and keep the hand moving.

meta.about: A waltz of our own for practicing a fingerpicking pattern. The thumb plays the root of each chord on beat 1, then the index, middle and ring fingers take the 3rd, 2nd and 1st strings and come back down, six even eighth notes per bar. The tune moves through the vamp twice, A7 to D7 to G: in G, that’s the same chord turn as D7–G7–C in C. Learn the pattern on a G chord first; then pick the tune, or have a friend pick it while you play the pattern.

meta.about: Many of the oldest banjo tunes from the Southern mountains are modal: they use a flat seventh, so in G you hear F instead of F♯, and the chords are just G and F. That gives tunes in the style of “Cluck Old Hen” and “Cumberland Gap” their lonesome, ringing sound. This one is our own. The first part sits on the 1st string, where the F is at the 3rd fret; the second part drops to the 4th string, where F is also at the 3rd fret. Every cell is a bum-ditty; where you see a hammer-on or pull-off, it fills the “and” after the strike.
meta.source: Original composition by Teddy Rook Book for this course (no source needed). It is written in the modal style of old Southern banjo tunes like “Cluck Old Hen” and “Cumberland Gap”, but the melody is our own.

meta.about: One of the best-loved pieces for classical guitar. Every beat is three notes: the ring finger (a) plays the tune on the 1st string, then the middle (m) and index (i) fingers play the 2nd and 3rd strings, while the thumb (p) plays a slow bass. Bring the tune out a little louder than the other two notes. The left hand travels: the tune climbs to the 12th fret in bar 5, uses a barre at the 5th fret for A minor and at the 7th fret for B7, then comes home to first position.

meta.about: In Travis picking the thumb swings back and forth between two bass strings on every beat, like a steady train, while the index and middle fingers pick a tune in the spaces between. On the C chord the thumb plays the 5th, 4th, 6th and 4th strings (the ring finger hops to the 3rd fret of the 6th string for the third beat). Learn the thumb part of each chord until it runs by itself, then add the fingers. Where a finger note lands on the beat with the thumb, pluck them together: that’s a pinch.
meta.source: Original composition by Teddy Rook Book for this course (no source needed); the style and the chord circle are traditional.
